sentences.text: Tonight I set two alarms for the new medication, and the second one is labeled just in case, which is also my whole life now. On the exam-table paper the specialist drew my immune system, little arrows attacking little circles, then tore it off for me to keep. Most of our savings went to the retainer, money we had set aside for a kitchen we will never renovate together. She left the wedding album on the curb with the recycling, and I carried it back inside without knowing why. Lab results arrive at midnight with no one to interpret them, just numbers glowing red outside their reference ranges. At soccer games we stand on opposite sidelines now, clapping for the same kid. Every morning now begins with a glass of water and a tablet the color of chalk. Forty pages signed on Tuesday, and I couldn't tell you what a single one of them said. Insurance kept me on hold for an hour, playing a jazz loop, while I decided which specialist I could afford. Half the internet says diet cures it; the other half posts photos of canes they've decorated with stickers. Two calendars now, one for work and one for whose week it is. I sorted a week of pills into the plastic organizer and thought, this is the furniture of my life now. Was it the year I traveled too much, or was it always coming? I've stopped pretending to know. At the grocery store I stood in the cereal aisle and could not remember what people who are fine buy. Forty minutes inside the MRI, knocking and humming, and I passed the time naming every room of my childhood house. Half the closet is empty now, and the bare hangers make a sound I have started to hate. Filing my response felt like agreeing to something I never chose. Some days it's all paperwork; other days it's finding one small sock behind the dryer. Every other Friday I pack a duffel bag for my daughter and pretend the zipper isn't the loudest thing in the house. Teal chairs, old magazines, a fish tank — the waiting room has become a place I could navigate blind. The rheumatologist said the word twice, calmly, and I watched her mouth move while the paper crinkled under my legs. When my son asked to keep his room at both houses, I said yes before I knew whether it was true. I practice saying "your mom and I both love you" in the mirror until it stops sounding rehearsed. Stuck to the fridge with a honeymoon magnet: the custody schedule, printed in her neat handwriting. My hands learned the injection routine faster than my mind did; they swab, pinch, press, done, while I look away. I told my landlord before I told my best friend, which says something I'm not ready to examine. Nobody at work knows yet; I ate lunch at my desk so the question of my face wouldn't come up. Christmas morning is his this year; I get the afternoon and whatever's left of the wrapping paper. Wednesday's appointment got moved to a month out, and I cried in the parking garage over a scheduling change. Behind the coffee punch card in my wallet sits the appointment card, ordinary and monstrous side by side. In the car I practiced saying the diagnosis out loud so it would stop sounding like someone else's news. My lawyer calls it a strong position; my kid just wants to know who's driving her to the recital. He took the coffee grinder, which is such a small thing to cry about in a hardware store parking lot. "Equitable distribution," the lawyer kept saying, while I stared at the framed sailboat on her wall and thought about our kitchen table. We told the kids at the kitchen table, and my daughter kept eating her cereal like she'd known for months. How do you answer "how are you" now — honestly, or in the old currency? Seven little doors on the pillbox, and closing each one feels like locking up a small shop at night. Did the pharmacist see the new prescription and understand what it meant, or am I the only one keeping score? Sunday nights after the handoff — that is the hour that hollows me out. There is a version of me from three weeks ago who complained about traffic; I think about her constantly. I want to write a suicide letter.
